changed_in.5.2: Closing the handle this call hands back now reports on the program rather than on the close, in the three values `os.execute()` gives: `true` or `nil` first, then `"exit"` or `"signal"` with the status or the signal number behind it — or, where the program could never be started, the system's own description and code in those same two positions. Earlier versions answer `true` on its own whenever the close itself went through, whatever the program made of its work, so there is no way through this handle to find out whether the work succeeded. Nothing about starting the program moved.
changed_in.5.3: `mode` is now checked before anything is started, and a spelling this call does not recognise raises instead of reaching the system. `"r"` and `"w"` are the pair every build recognises; whether a build takes anything after them is a setting that build chooses, so those two on their own are the portable spellings. Earlier versions hand the string over exactly as written, and a spelling the system will not have is reported the way any failure to start is — a false value, a message and a code — rather than as a mistake in the call.
changed_in.5.4: The handle can now be held in a to-be-closed variable. The metatable for file handles gained a `__close` metamethod beside the finalizer it has always carried, so `local reported <close> = assert(io.popen(command))` gives the handle up when the block ends, however it ends. On this handle that costs more than it does on a file: the close waits for the program to finish, so the block does not end until it has — and the three values describing how it ended are discarded, because a to-be-closed variable has nowhere to put them. A program that wants the status still closes by hand. Earlier versions have no such declaration at all.
